TXPIN = SR_TRIG, PINOE = SR_TRIG
which is the act's own derivation and the
datasheet's 10 us minimum exactly.
MEASURED 601 CLOCKS = 10.0167 us.
One clock long. The device asks for a MINIMUM so
this is harmless to a real sensor, and the check
is an equality anyway because the act claims the
COUNT rather than a datasheet floor.
the trigger
the counted delay, then release
recovery, then 8 x 40 kHz, then ECHO HIGH
The firmware does not look at the 8 bursts: it
cannot resynchronise to a burst it did not send.
THE ANSWER IS THE WIDTH OF THE PULSE, not a level,
which is what makes this act safe at 4 m - a width
does not care when you looked at it.
spin until the echo goes HIGH
THE ECHO IS CAPTURED, NOT SAMPLED.
The counter
is RESET at this edge and READ at the falling edge,
so there is no 16-bit subtract - and this machine
has no carry flag, so a subtract is a four-case
analysis on bit 7 and a compare is the same
analysis again. One reset removes both.
read the COUNTER, not the flag
THE 1 us COUNTER, read as a DIFFERENCE
- exactly as
in freqmeter.pe, for the same reason: the clear-on-read
flag on port 6 is ONE BIT, so a poll loop longer than a
tick reports several ticks as one, and the loss is
invisible in the result.
Port 7 is the 4.33 us UART half-bit tick and is not a
microsecond.
now
t = the accumulated microseconds
MEASURED 1160 us
against the model's 1 160 us -
EXACT
, and the check is 1 % with a 2 us floor.
mm = us * 11/64, exactly
us = 64q + r, so us*11/64 = 11q + floor(11r/64), exactly,
because 11q is an integer. Four doublings and two adds
for each multiply by eleven, no loop and no second
temporary.
THE CONVERSION IS EXACT, AND IT IS THE ACT.
The
testbench asserts it as an equality, not a window.
bank it, dmem[10] = 1
measurement 1: this one does not
the echo for the second target
THE MODEL PREPARED 5 816 us -> expect 999 mm.
The large target is the one that makes the act worth
running: 1 160 us fits in twelve bits and 5 816 us
does not, so the pair exercises the ten-bit path AND
the high byte. A single near target would prove the
conversion works and say nothing about the case that
could overflow - and an overflow in the high byte is
invisible from the outside, because the answer would
still be a plausible millimetre figure.
FAIL: THE MODEL SAW EXACTLY 1 TRIGGER, NOT 2.
The check carries its own explanation in the TB: "a
trigger that is driven rather than pulsed shows up
here" - which is the right way to write a failing
check, because the reader learns the SHAPE of the
defect from the message instead of going to hunt for
it in the design.
FAIL: dmem[10] = 01. THE FIRMWARE BANKED ONE
MEASUREMENT.
and the second reading is still the FIRST one's:
measurement 1: echo 5816 us -> firmware 1160 us
THE FAILURE IS UPSTREAM OF THE CONVERSION.
The
arithmetic is exact on the measurement that ran, and
every failing check is about the second measurement
not happening rather than about the answer being
wrong.
the open defect, and what is NOT claimed
WHAT IS KNOWN:
the second measurement is lost, the bank holds one result,
the model saw one trigger, and the trigger is one clock long.
WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED:
which instruction is wrong. The five failing checks
say the second measurement does not happen; they do not say why, and a figure
that drew a cause would be drawing a hypothesis presented as a finding.
WHERE TO LOOK FIRST:
the 601-vs-600 trigger, because it is a
one-instruction error of exactly the kind this family has found six times, and
because it sits in the path that issues the second trigger and re-arms for the
second echo. Stated as a place to look, not as the fault.
WHAT IS NOT IN THE REGRESSION:
tb_pe_soc_sr04.v is tracked but NOT wired
into regress/run_all.sh, so a green gate says nothing about this act in either
direction. The act's own state has to be read from running it, and running it is
how this page's numbers were obtained.

AND NOTE WHAT IS NOT IN THE TABLE.
No row says the conversion is wrong,
because no conversion check failed. A red table that mixes a proven property with
a broken one, and does not say which is which, is worse than a red table: the
reader cannot tell whether to trust the arithmetic or distrust it.
